opus-5.5.text:
I think we're still early, but we're past the point where the question is whether reasoning works. When we started on what became the o1 line of models, the bet was that you could take a pretrained model and teach it, through reinforcement learning, to think for longer before answering, and that the extra thinking would turn into real capability. That bet has paid off. You can see it most clearly in math and competitive programming, where problems have verifiable answers and the model can learn from getting things right or wrong.

So the core idea is established. What's still open is how far it generalizes. In domains with a clean reward signal, like math, code, and some science, progress is fast and I expect it to continue. The harder question is the messier domains, where there's no unit test to tell you whether you got it right. How do you train a model to reason well about a business strategy, or a piece of writing, or an ambiguous research direction? That's where much of the interesting work is now.

The other thing I'd point out is that reasoning shifts where compute goes. For years the scaling story was mostly about pretraining: bigger models, more data. Now there's a second axis, test-time compute, where you let the model spend more effort on the problem in front of it. That changes the economics. Some tasks are worth a lot of thinking, and now you can pay for that thinking when it matters.

My overall take is that we've found a new scaling dimension, and we're in the phase where that becomes obvious to everyone. The coming years will be about extending it from verifiable problems into the much larger space of things people actually want done, and about turning reasoning into agents that can carry out long, multi-step work reliably. That last part, reliability over long horizons, is the piece I'd watch most closely.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say we're really at the beginning of it. If you think about the history of what we've done with language models, the first big phase was pre-training—scaling up models on more and more data, and watching capabilities emerge almost as a byproduct. That took us a long way, but it has a ceiling in the sense that you're essentially asking the model to answer instantly, in one pass, whatever you put in front of it.

Reasoning is a different axis. It's about giving the model time to think—to work through a problem step by step, consider alternatives, notice when it's made a mistake, and go back. When we started working on this seriously, it was clear pretty quickly that the gains were real. The o1 work showed that if you train a model to use that thinking time well, you get large jumps on hard problems in math, coding, and science—the kinds of problems where a single forward pass just isn't enough.

But I'd emphasize how early it still is. A few things stand out to me. First, the scaling story for reasoning is just getting started. With pre-training, we spent years learning how far the curve went. With test-time compute, we've only begun to push on it, and so far the returns keep coming. Second, the reasoning we see today is strongest in domains where there's a clear right answer you can check—math problems, code that passes tests. The open question is how well it generalizes to messier domains where the feedback is fuzzier: writing, strategy, scientific judgment. I'm optimistic, but that's still being worked out. And third, we haven't really connected reasoning to action at scale yet. The next big step is agents—models that reason over long horizons, take actions in the world, see the results, and adjust. That requires reliability over many steps, and that's where a lot of the hard research is going to be.

So if I had to put it in a frame: pre-training got us models that know a lot. Reasoning is getting us models that can think. The stage after that is models that can actually do things over long stretches of time without falling over. We're in the middle of the second phase and just starting the third, and I think the next few years are going to look very different from the last few because of it.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re still early. We’ve made a lot of progress in getting models to give useful answers, but reasoning asks something more: can a model work through a problem, recognize when an approach isn’t working, and try something else?

One of the exciting directions is giving models more time to think. Humans don’t solve every problem in one pass, and there’s no reason to expect that to be the best approach for AI either. But spending more time only helps if the model uses that time productively. It needs to check its work and make progress, rather than just produce a longer answer.

So I’d distinguish promising demonstrations from dependable reasoning. The research question is how to turn those promising capabilities into something that works reliably across unfamiliar problems. I think there’s a lot of room left to improve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re still very early, but we’ve reached an important turning point. For a long time, progress mostly came from training larger models on more data. Now we’re seeing that you can also improve a model’s answers by giving it more time to work through a problem—trying different approaches, checking its work, and correcting mistakes.

That opens up a new research direction: how do you train models to use that extra computation effectively? And how do they decide which problems need a quick answer and which deserve more thought? We’ve seen encouraging progress on problems where you can check the answer, like math and coding. The bigger question is how well those capabilities transfer to messy, open-ended problems. So I’m excited about the direction, but I think there’s a lot left to discover.
